content: Olaflur, also known as amine fluoride 297, is a fluoride-containing compound that has been utilized as an active ingredient in toothpastes and dental solutions since 1966. Its primary purpose is to prevent dental caries. When combined with dectaflur, olaflur is also formulated into gels that are used for treating early stages of dental caries, managing tooth sensitivity, and refluoridating damaged enamel. These gels are often applied by dental professionals. Excessive use of olaflur can result in irritation of the oral mucosa. In individuals with heightened sensitivity, even standard doses may provoke irritation. Like other fluoride salts, olaflur is toxic when administered in high doses over prolonged periods. In children, particularly before the eruption of permanent teeth, overdosage can lead to dental fluorosis, a condition characterized by discoloration and weakening of the enamel. In acute cases of overdose, such as accidental ingestion of olaflur-containing products, calcium in any oral form can act as an antidote. Milk is commonly used in such situations due to its ready availability. Calcium-containing drugs and foods can inhibit the action of olaflur because calcium fluoride is practically insoluble in water. Chemically, olaflur is a salt composed of an alkyl ammonium cation and fluoride as the counterion. The cation, with its long lipophilic hydrocarbon chain, exhibits surfactant properties. It forms a film on the surface of teeth, which facilitates the incorporation of fluoride into the enamel. This process converts the outer layers of hydroxyapatite, the primary mineral in enamel, into the more durable fluorapatite. However, the fluoridation effect is limited to a depth of only a few nanometers, raising questions about whether the mechanism truly depends on fluorapatite formation. The synthesis of olaflur begins with cattle tallow, from which fatty acids, primarily stearic acid (C17H35COOH), are obtained through hydrolysis. These fatty acids are converted into their corresponding amides, which are then catalytically reduced to primary amines. Acrylonitrile is added, followed by another reduction step, yielding N-alkyl-1,3-propanediamines. The nitrogen atoms in these compounds react with ethylene oxide (oxirane) to form tertiary amines. Finally, hydrofluoric acid is introduced to produce the final product. Since olaflur is synthesized from a mixture of fatty acids, some molecules may have side chains that are longer or shorter than 18 carbon atoms. Byproducts of the reaction include hydroxyethyl ethers, which result from the addition of ethylene oxide to free hydroxyl groups. However, the presence of these byproducts is clinically insignificant.
